conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what happened before you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I was at home yesterday afternoon and started feeling really lightheaded, like I was going to pass out. I called my neighbor, and when I woke up, I was on the floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How long do you think you were unconscious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure—maybe a few minutes? I remember calling my neighbor, then nothing until she found me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations before it happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the dizziness. And I’ve been feeling kind of off balance since—like I’m drunk when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea, vision changes, or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, but I do have a headache on the left side. Not the worst I’ve ever had, but it’s there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You mentioned poor appetite—did you eat much the day before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I wasn’t feeling well, so I didn’t eat much. But I did take my glyburide that morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even though you hadn’t eaten?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But it didn’t feel like my usual low blood sugar—no shaking or sweating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll check your glucose and keep an eye on that. We also did an EKG, and it showed some changes in the heart tracing, but your cardiac enzymes were normal, so it’s unlikely a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Should I be worried about my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. The changes could be due to your high blood pressure or other factors. We’re monitoring you on telemetry, and no arrhythmias have shown up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a CT scan of your head last night—no bleeding or stroke. But because of your balance issues, neurology recommended an MRI and MRA, which we did this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did they show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No acute stroke or tumor. But there are signs of small vessel disease in the brain, which is common with high blood pressure and diabetes. Also, there’s mild narrowing at the start of the right vertebral artery, but it’s not severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I fell?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the neurology team doesn’t think it caused a stroke. Given your recent cold symptoms—cough, congestion—the leading thought is labyrinthitis, an inner ear issue that affects balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t think of that. I’ve had a stuffy nose for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. Labyrinthitis can cause dizziness, imbalance, and even a brief loss of consciousness in some cases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your urine test results back. It showed cocaine use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I haven’t used it recently. Maybe a few weeks ago. I know it’s not good, but I’m trying to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate your honesty. Cocaine can cause serious heart issues, especially with high blood pressure. It can also trigger arrhythmias or worsen artery narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. I didn’t know it could affect my heart like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. Because of this, we’re stopping your propranolol. Combining it with cocaine can increase the risk of severe high blood pressure or heart complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I take that for my headaches. Will I get more of them now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on topiramate and acetazolamide, which also help with migraines and pseudotumor. We’ll discuss long-term options with your neurologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was high when you came in—172 over 100. We restarted your enalapril and amlodipine, and it’s now well-controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been skipping my BP meds sometimes when I feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but with your history, it’s important to take them daily. High blood pressure increases stroke and heart risks, especially with your other conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do better. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your labs are stable, imaging shows no acute issues, and your balance is a bit better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But I’m still a little wobbly. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can take time to recover from labyrinthitis. A physical therapist will come to your home for gait and balance training.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your usual meds except propranolol—we’re stopping that permanently due to the cocaine use. All others are adjusted slightly, and instructions are in your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should stop using cocaine for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. It’s dangerous for your heart and brain. Please consider speaking with a counselor or support group—we can help connect you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep those follow-up appointments.
